text: Actors rehearsing a Passion play in Montreal find the parts following them home. Denys Arcand keeps the comedy and the ache in one room: a company of working performers agrees to stage the oldest story in the city's Catholic memory, then decides to take the research seriously. That second decision turns a job into a conflict, since the Church that considers the story its property has no appetite for interpretation. Canada's film academy gave the picture its best-motion-picture award, and a festival jury added its prize. Neither fact conveys the tone, which sits closer to farce than to reverence for a good while. Over 119 minutes the rehearsals and the private lives run alongside one another, and the film never once points at the resemblance.

A wool cooperative and a small clinic are the whole of what two people from Buenos Aires have built in a remote Argentine valley. Mario teaches, Ana runs the clinic with a nun named Nelda, and their twelve-year-old son is growing up inside an arrangement he did not choose. Then a Spanish geologist arrives with instruments and a contract from the local landowner, hired to determine whether the valley can be flooded for hydro-electric power. Adolfo Aristarain builds the drama out of surveying, which sounds inert and is not: every measurement is an argument about whether the people here get to stay, or are moved into the cities. Hans has no illusions left and says so. The household has plenty and lives by them, which is the more exposed position, and the film knows it.

Jettel Redlich packs the china and an evening gown, and that is how she arrives in Kenya. She has fled Nazi Germany with her daughter to join a husband already working a farm, and her refusal of the place is the engine of the film rather than an obstacle it clears in a reel. Caroline Link takes 140 minutes, roughly the time required to rebuild a marriage on terms nobody in it would have chosen. The daughter moves faster. Regina learns the country through Owuor, the cook, and the friendship is filmed as a relationship between two people rather than as instruction. What is at stake is not survival alone but the shape of an ordinary life, dishes and language and what a household expects at dinner, carried into a place with no use for any of it.

The work is clerical, tidying a politician's memoirs against a deadline, and the man who had the job before drowned. Roman Polanski keeps nearly the whole thriller on a remote island and inside a manuscript, so the suspense has to be built from reading and from the courtesies of a household that has already had one accident. Adam Lang, lately Prime Minister of Britain, is available for as many hours as the book requires, and that availability becomes its own kind of pressure. The film is a French production spoken in English, which suits a story about a man employed to write in another man's voice. French prizes went to the adaptation, the score and the direction, which also took a Silver Bear. Two hours of politeness, thinning.

Men here settle a quarrel by taking turns hitting each other until one of them stays down. Zacharias Kunuk films that, along with the seal-oil lamps and the walrus meat and the long haul to the caribou hunt, as ordinary practice rather than as exhibit: the camera lives in the household instead of visiting it. The story is a legend from the region, spoken in Inuktitut and performed by Inuit actors, and it turns on love, jealousy and who is permitted to hold power inside a group too small to lose anyone. The 172 minutes are not indulgence. A hunt takes the time it takes, and the film's patience is the argument rather than a manner. It won the Caméra d'Or, and Toronto later put it on its all-time Canadian ten.

A mother sells her daughter to a traveling strongman, and the daughter goes. Federico Fellini declines to treat the transaction as exceptional: Zampanò works his act village by village for coins, Gelsomina learns the routine and the roads, and the cruelty between them is intermittent and domestic, which is worse than spectacular. Il Matto, a clown on the same circuit, opens a second possibility for her without ever promising it. The scale is deliberately small, two performers and a road and crowds that do not stay, and the 115 minutes go to temperament rather than incident. Directors have kept it on the Sight & Sound poll for decades and Italy lists it among the films it means to preserve, but the thing that holds is plainer: a woman's loyalty examined until the word stops sounding like a compliment.

The women break the village radio first, and then the television. Around them a country is splitting along the line between Muslim and Christian; inside the village the two have lived together, and the women have concluded that news is the thing most likely to end that. Nadine Labaki plays long stretches as comedy, which is the harder choice, since the farce depends on men being kept occupied and misinformed for their own survival. Land mines ring the village, so nobody is leaving, and the film uses the enclosure the way a stage uses walls. It took the François Chalais Prize and an audience award. Arabic, 110 minutes, and a chain of improvisations, each holding only until the next piece of news gets through.

Everything on screen has been dragged into the present except the words. Baz Luhrmann relocates the Montagues and Capulets to a sweltering coastal suburb called Verona Beach and leaves the verse untouched, which obliges the cast to deliver Elizabethan lines at the tempo of a modern quarrel. That friction is both the method and the risk. When it works, the language stops sounding like an assignment; when it slips, the seams show from a distance. The production design carries much of the weight, and it is the craft the Academy singled out, because the world has to be readable at a glance for the trick to survive. Two hours, cut fast, pitched at a speed no stage can manage. Whether that is adaptation or transfusion is a fair argument, and the film is not coy about its side.

The clock is the structure: a man has a date with the state, and a nun has agreed to sit with him until it arrives. Between the two of them lie the murders of a young couple, and Tim Robbins gives that fact the same weight he gives the fear of the man now waiting in a cell for the sentence to be carried out. What the nun offers is attention rather than absolution, which is the harder thing to sit through, since it obliges everyone in the frame to keep looking at a person they would rather file away. The film runs 122 minutes and spends nearly all of them counting down. Both lead performances were recognized in Hollywood and at Berlin, and the reason is legible in the design: the drama is conversation, in rooms, on a schedule set by a warrant.

Two men share a deck and agree on nothing; one holds the command, the other holds the crew's regard. Frank Lloyd spends the early stretch of his 1935 adventure on discipline, how it is administered, who is made to watch, what the watching costs, and that patience is why the Bounty feels like a place of work rather than a set. Fletcher Christian is the officer caught between two loyalties. Captain Bligh is the reason a choice exists at all. Made when a sea story had to be staged on actual water, it runs 132 minutes of rope, weather and rank. It was named best picture of its year and still sits on the standard lists of films to see. What keeps it upright now is smaller than the mutiny: a chain of command filmed as a moral situation rather than a chart.

Jekyll's theory is that a man contains two men, and that separating them would be a mercy. Rouben Mamoulian took the idea up in 1931, while American horror was still deciding what it was permitted to show, and the picture is franker about appetite than the decade after it would allow. Ninety-six minutes, brisk for a story carrying this much apparatus; the length goes to the doctor's reasoning, and to how quickly reasoning hardens into habit. The monster is not the interesting problem here. The gentleman's certainty that his experiment serves the public good is, and the respectability that funds the second life keeps drawing the camera back. Academy attention went to the lead performance and the cinematography, and both are load-bearing: a film built on a face and on what light is allowed to do to it.

She sends for the gunman whose name everyone knows, and the man who arrives does not match it. Cat Ballou takes the revenge plot — a murdered father, a hired gun, a debt to collect — and treats it as a straight line on which to hang jokes. That was a workable position by 1965, when the Western had repeated its routines long enough that an audience could call the beats before the characters did. The comedy is affectionate rather than corrosive; the genre is being enjoyed out loud, at 97 minutes, with a cutting rhythm built for the gag rather than the draw. The Academy recognized the lead performance. The odder achievement is structural: the revenge belongs to a young woman, and the film never quietly hands it to the man she hired.

1940, New York: a saxophone player arrives and is noticed almost at once. Clint Eastwood gives Charlie 'Bird' Parker 161 minutes, long for a musician's life and about right for a film willing to let a number play to its end. A film about a musician has to solve one problem before any other, which is whether the playing sounds like the thing being praised. Of all the craft the picture was honored for, the award for sound is the telling one: the bandstand is where the case gets made, and the addiction underneath is measured against what happens when the horn is working. Chan is a participant rather than a witness, and the help she offers is practical. The film stays beside the man through the hours the music actually takes.

The safest place a widow can think of is the village she came from, so she takes her daughter and goes. Vittorio De Sica made La ciociara in 1961, a decade and a half after the war it describes, and kept the scale domestic: a mother, a girl of twelve, a rural hometown, the daily arithmetic of food and shelter and whom to trust. It is spoken in Italian and registered as a French production. The performance at the center took the Academy's award for actress, and it is not a decorous piece of work; the woman is practical before she is anything else, and the film respects her for that. A hundred minutes, and for most of them the war is still a rumor at their backs, closing.
